sections.abstract: The paper introduces I-Con (Information Contrastive Learning), a unifying information-theoretic framework for representation learning. It presents a single equation that generalizes a large collection of modern loss functions by minimizing an integrated KL divergence between two conditional distributions: the supervisory representation ($p_{\theta}$) and the learned representation ($q_{\phi}$). This framework unifies over 23 different approaches, including clustering, spectral methods, dimensionality reduction, contrastive learning, and supervised learning. The authors demonstrate that I-Con can be used to derive new loss functions and principled debiasing methods, achieving a +8% improvement over state-of-the-art unsupervised image classifiers on ImageNet-1K.
sections.introduction: The field of representation learning has seen a proliferation of diverse loss functions, making it difficult to understand their relationships. I-Con provides a mathematical framework that unifies these seemingly disparate methods under a single objective. The authors prove 15 theorems showing how various algorithms emerge as special cases of I-Con. Key contributions include the introduction of the I-Con loss, theoretical proofs for 23 distinct methods, and the development of a debiasing strategy that significantly improves unsupervised classification accuracy on benchmarks like ImageNet-1K (+8%), CIFAR-100 (+3%), and STL-10 (+2%).
sections.method: The paper reviews foundational and recent work across several areas: 1) Feature Learning (e.g., PCA, MDS, UMAP, t-SNE) which aims to derive informative low-dimensional embeddings; 2) Contrastive Learning (e.g., SimCLR, CMC, CLIP, MoCo v3) which uses positive and negative pairs; 3) Clustering (e.g., k-Means, spectral clustering, SCAN, TEMI) which uncovers discrete structures; and 4) Unifying Representation Learning, noting that while prior work has linked small subsets of these methods, I-Con is the first to provide a broad unification under a single information-theoretic objective. The I-Con framework unifies representation learning by minimizing the average KL divergence between a supervisory neighborhood distribution $p_{\theta}(j|i)$ and a learnable distribution $q_{\phi}(j|i)$. The core loss function is defined as: $$\mathcal{L}(\theta, \phi) = \int_{i \in \mathcal{X}} D_{KL} (p_{\theta}(\cdot|i)||q_{\phi}(\cdot|i)) = \int_{i \in \mathcal{X}} \int_{j \in \mathcal{X}} p_{\theta}(j|i) \log \frac{p_{\theta}(j|i)}{q_{\phi}(j|i)}$$ (Eq. 1). By varying the construction of these distributions, I-Con recovers methods like SNE (Gaussian vs. Gaussian), SimCLR (augmentations as neighbors), and K-Means (cluster membership as neighbors). The paper introduces two debiasing strategies: 1) Uniform Distribution Mixture: $\tilde{p}(j|i) = (1 - \alpha) p(j|i) + \frac{\alpha}{N}$, which mitigates overconfident allocations similar to label smoothing; and 2) Neighbor Propagation: expanding neighborhoods via graph walks, defined as $\tilde{P} \propto P + P^2 + \dots + P^k$ or a uniform version $\tilde{P}_U \propto I[P + P^2 + \dots + P^k > 0]$.
sections.experiments: The authors evaluate I-Con on the ImageNet-1K dataset using Hungarian accuracy as the primary metric. They utilize DiNO pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT) models (S/14, B/14, L/14) for feature extraction and train a linear classifier for 30 epochs. Baselines include TEMI, SCAN, IIC, and Contrastive Clustering. The proposed 'InfoNCE Clustering' incorporates augmentations, KNNs ($k=3$), and KNN walks.
sections.results: Results show that Debiased InfoNCE Clustering significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art, achieving 57.8% (ViT-S), 64.75% (ViT-B), and 67.52% (ViT-L) accuracy. Ablation studies confirm that debiasing, KNN propagation, and EMA stabilization all contribute to performance gains. Neighbor propagation (1 or 2 walks) is particularly effective at capturing local structure.
sections.conclusion: I-Con provides a unified information-theoretic perspective on representation learning, acting as a 'periodic table' of machine learning losses. It proves that many popular loss functions are special cases of a single KL divergence objective. This unification not only clarifies existing methods but also enables the transfer of techniques across domains, leading to state-of-the-art results in unsupervised image classification and principled debiasing methods for contrastive learners.
sections.supplementary: The supplementary material contains detailed proofs and additional experimental results. Appendix A provides further evaluations on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, STL-10, and Oxford-IIIT Pet, showing that debiasing consistently improves accuracy across different backbones and distribution types (Gaussian vs. Student-t). Appendix B contains proofs for dimensionality reduction methods, including Theorem 1 (SNE), Corollary 1 (t-SNE), Proposition 1 (Cohesion Variance Loss), and Theorem 2 (PCA). Appendix C details proofs for feature learning methods: Theorem 3 (InfoNCE), Corollary 2 (t-SimCLR/t-SimCNE), Theorem 4 (VICReg), Theorem 5 (Triplet Loss), Theorem 6 (SupCon), Theorem 7 (X-Sample), Theorem 8 (CMC/CLIP), Theorem 9 (Cross-Entropy), Theorem 10 (Harmonic Loss), and Theorem 11 (MLM). Appendix D focuses on clustering: Definition 1 (Classical K-means), Proposition 2 (Probabilistic Relaxation), Theorem 12 (Contrastive Formulation), Theorem 13 (K-means as I-Con), Corollary 4 (Spectral Clustering), Theorem 14 (Normalized Cuts), and Theorem 15 (Mutual Information Clustering). Appendix E frames I-Con as a variational method, connecting it to Mutual Information and Variational Bayesian (VB) methods: $$\mathcal{L}(\phi) = \int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \text{KL}(p(z|x)||q_{\phi}(z)) dx$$ (Eq. 13). Appendix F discusses the necessity of unification. Appendix G provides a guide for choosing neighborhood distributions. Appendix H compares I-Con with MLE and standard KL divergence. Appendix I discusses I-Con's hyperparameters, noting its self-balancing nature which removes the need for manual tuning of entropy penalties or EMA stabilization.
